Phaedrus reflected on the destruction of the laboratory. It appears that while the force device was powerful, its use as a weapon was questionable. Oh well, such was the way of research. Sometimes you get an expected result that leads to a real life solution, other times you find a different result and a solution to another problem, one that sometimes hasn`t even been thought of yet.

What was discovered? Force is met by force. If something acts, it is acted against. One object cannot interact with another without being interacted with in turn. Such a thought was interesting, and perhaps the force circuit could be made into an effective means of propulsion.

In the meantime, there was still the weapon problem, and he was back at square one. Oh well, life happens. Maybe he should check on another division, crystal clips and buttons were all the rage these days, maybe the department of Crystallography could have made an interesting development.

*****

Ever since Floatstone synthesis had begun, the Spectra had gained an interest in crystal synthesis. In the newly emerging field, one promising researcher quickly rose through the ranks. Claudia, director of the Crystallographic division, was at the top of the world. Her life had been going great, progress was going swimmingly, while mild developments had been made.

And then Phaedrus showed up.

Phaedrus was famous amongst the circles in the Order of Moonlight. The Director of Moonlight himself, eccentric, wild, and rather rude. A visit from Phaedrus usually spelled bad news, and will at the very least ruin your day.

When Phaedrus showed up unannounced into her laboratory, Claudia was vexed, then immediately horrified. Disaster followed where Phaedrus went, she had to get him out of here fast.

"Ahh, Phaedrus, to what do we owe the pleasure of your appeareance?"

Phaedrus indicated surprise, then replied.

"Don't bother with pleasantries, you can't even hide that you don't want me here. I expected more from one of the Directors."

"Why are you here Phaedrus?" Claudia sighed.

"Just checking in, I've hit a dead-end in what I was doing, so just taking a walk, seeing if I could get some new ideas. Better to discuss this outside the lab space, don't want to disturb the delicate work you're doing here."

Claudia had a sigh of relief. "Yes, lets. I'd rather that you didn't destroy our instruments simply by appearing here."

*****

Phaedrus was examining a set of crystal rods. One was clear, the other a shade of crimson red.

"So, you said you used the same material to make both of these?"

Claudia hesitated, she didn't understand how this was remotely difficult to understand.

"As far as I know, yes, I could check the records, hold on."

Claudia dug through the archives until she found the crystal she was looking for.

"Here, this was the log for that day. As you see, the experiments should have been identical."

"Then what was this report of a laboratory accident?" Phaedrus pointed out.

"Mild traces of a metalic impurity, that was tossed into the crystal production apparatus, the amounts were low enough that we considered it insignificant."

"And yet it seems to have made a substantial difference. Something in that impurity gave it some, odd properties. If you pass white light through, it becomes red."

Phaedrus rose, and spoke again.

"I want you to find out what impurity this was, and maybe to try again. This is certainly very pretty. At the very least, this could be profitable. I guess we could divert some more resources into your division, great more paperwork."

Claudia could hardly believe this was happening. A Phaedrus meeting that DIDN'T end in disaster. Oh she would have a story to tell to her fellow co-workers. Not only that, but she had the entire thing on record, could make and win some bets with this.

Phaedrus' voice snapped her out of her reverie.

"If it isn't too much to ask, I would love to take this rod. You will be suitably compensated for this inconvenience."

Claudia was in high spirits, and felt the rod was not of much value anyways. She saw no reason to refuse.

"Yeah, sure, go right ahead. Thank you so much for your visit."

*****

Back in his study, Phaedrus took the rod, and the circuit that made the air glow. After building a quick housing, and inserting the crystal, he flipped the switch.

To his eternal satisfaction, the rod slowly began to glow.

To Phaedrus, just as it had been apparant to Luminus, light was power. Light was an instrument of destruction and harm. It was a harbinger of hope. He smiled, and got back to work.

Phaedrus had hit a dead end, but discovered Newton's third law of motion. Needing a distraction, he pays a surprise visit to Claudia, Director of the Department of Crystallography. After a meeting, Phaedrus discovers a strange property leading to colour being introduced to a crystal, and orders production of a number of crimson red crystal rods, as well as diverting additional resources. Phaedrus then takes the rod and energizes it, seeing a faint glow come from the rod.

If you play a reasonably-optimized 3D game, you'll notice that it can render hundreds of different textures without any problem, even if they're not the largest ones. However, put the same textures on a web browser and it may be possible that the browser will slow down to a crawl or even crash, especially when rendering images larger than 10000Ã—10000 pixels, even if 3D games can handle them with no problem, even if they have to bend and twist those textures.

Why is that? Can web browsers be optimized, using good parts of game engines?
[Question] How come that many video games can handle processing images much faster than common web browsers?
I think it has to do with the API used and access to GPU resources. A web browser isn't likely to look for 3D acceleration from a GTX980, it's just going to run on a single thread on a CPU.
That's what Hardware Acceleration is in this case. In fact, Chrome has that. It's enabled by default. It's only for videos though and some specific browser games (like Unity based games).

It's all down to design. Web browsers aren't meant to load large textures, while the game is.

Also if I'm not mistaken the browser would only take ahold of the CPU and wouldn't know what to do with a GPU.
Are you not perhaps confusing rendering the textures with downloading the textures? Because that takes time.

Some of the answers here are correct, others are wrong.

I work for a fairly large dot com as a product manager owning heavily accessed portions of our site. Metrics are pretty clear - we rapidly lose money if things are slow to load. I have at least a dozen new bug reports each weak related to bizarre or slow behavior specific to a browser and obsess constantly over speeding things up.

One of the greatest things that happened for Windows, back in the day, was the transition from Winforms (old school grey/blocky looking windows applications) to Windows Presentation Foundation (WPF). If nothing else, it shifted the apps to use the GPU where possible, and fall back onto the software rasterizer where not. The practical effect of this in many cases, was your rotations, scrolling, etc. was executing on your gpu as 2d/3d transforms, etc.

Many (most?) modern web browsers, nowadays, do use GPU rendering for quite a large number of things. Some of the behavior you're describing above is the result of web browsers attempting to aggressively optimize performance. We had an issue recently, for example, where only chrome behaved poorly with extremely large images, due to some behind the scenes optimization non-sense it was attempting to do.

A lot of what you probably experience, however, is the result of javascript, which is literally the devil, being unperformant and bad in all ways, and AJAX calls happening in the background.
